To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) HPV infection is a cause of cervical and other anogenital cancers and of oropharyngeal cancers; (2) HPV infection may cause a subset of head and neck cancers that are not oropharyngeally derived; and (3) HPV infection does not cause cancers of the lung, esophagus, or liver.
HPV infection of the uterine cervix causes 100% of cervical cancers and that HPV infection of oral mucosa, larynx, esophagus, and anus may cause a subset of these cancers.
(1) HPV is associated with cancers at nongeneral sites, (2) this association is biologically plausible, and (3) the association is supported by epidemiologic and molecular data.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification, characterization, and evaluation of the role of mucosal-type HPV infections as a risk factor for human cancer.
understanding the etiologic role of HPV in human cancer.
the role of HPV in cancers of the head and neck, esophagus, lung, and liver.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is insufficient evidence to conclude that mucosal HPV infection plays an etiologic role in the pathogenesis of any nongenital cancer, but the evidence is sufficient to warrant further investigation
there is no evidence that mucosal HPV infection causes cancer at nongenitally located sites, although the possibility cannot be excluded.

, at this time, there is sufficient evidence to suggest a possible causal role for mucosal-type HPV in the etiology of a subset of cancers of the oral cavity, oropharynx, larynx, esophagus, lung, breast, prostate, and cervix.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, although the evidence is still incomplete, it is reasonable to hypothesize that mucosal-type HPV infections play a role in the etiology of some nongenital tract cancers, particularly those of the head and neck and the anal region.
the evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that mucosal HPV infection plays a causal role in some, but not all, nongenital HPV-related cancers.

the epidemiologic and biologic evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that mucosal HPV is a cofactor in the pathogenesis of a number of nongenital malignancies, including a significant fraction of head and neck, esophageal, and lung cancers.
The main takeaway from our work is that

, in addition to cervical cancer and oropharyngeal cancer, HPV is a causal factor in anal cancer, and that HPV may also be a causal factor in penile, vaginal, vulvar, and possibly some nonmelanoma skin cancers.
HPV is a likely cause of cancers of the anus, oropharynx, penis, and vagina, but the evidence is not as strong for other nongenial cancers.
the epidemiology of nongenital HPV-associated cancers, as well as the biological characteristics of the virus, is highly consistent with a causal relationship.
